title: Salmacis
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Alcithoë, one of the daughters of Minyas, takes her turn at the loom and offers to explain why the spring of Salmacis leaves the limbs of any man who bathes in it soft. A boy born to Mercury and the goddess of Cythera, reared by naiads on Ida, comes at fifteen to a pool kept by a nymph who will not hunt and spends her days consulting the water about her own looks; she asks him for his bed, is refused, pretends to leave, and takes hold of him when he has undressed and swum. Her prayer that no day part them is granted to the letter, and the two bodies close into one that can be called neither woman nor boy. The tale ends and the sisters go on weaving — until drums no one can see sound in the house, the webs put out ivy, and the sisters go into the dark on wings and take a name from the evening.

advisory.lede: Salmacis sexually assaults a boy who has refused her, and the tale makes the two-sexed body that results a curse: it is an origin story both for a spring said to unman any man who bathes in it and for the word hermaphrodite, long used of intersex people.
advisory.more: The boy tells Salmacis to stop and threatens to leave; she pretends to go, hides, and takes hold of him when he has undressed and swum. Ovid does not hurry any of it: kisses are snatched while he struggles, the chest she touches is called unwilling, and three similes in a row — an eagle carrying off a snake, ivy round a trunk, an octopus round its prey — describe the grip. What follows is a fusion he did not ask for, and the poem's own words for the result are hostile: semimarem, half-male, and semivir, which was a Roman insult, with the doctored spring called incestus, unclean. That vocabulary belongs to the tale and to its narrator, one of the sisters who are punished a few lines later. Lectorium presents the text unaltered and does not soften the translation.

sentences.t: Dixerat, et factum mirabile ceperat aures.
sentences.l: She had spoken, and the marvellous deed had caught [their] ears.
sentences.i: She had ended, and the marvel of it had caught their ears.
sentences.n: Two pluperfects (dixerat, ceperat) drop the curtain between one sister's tale and the next: the telling is over before the sentence begins. “ceperat aures” — it took their ears, the ears standing in for the listeners and their attention.

sentences.t:
Pars fieri potuisse negant, pars omnia veros
posse deos memorant: sed non et Bacchus in illis.
sentences.l: Part deny that it could have happened, part relate that the true gods can [do] all things: but Bacchus [is] not also among them.
sentences.i: Some deny it could have happened; others say the true gods can do anything — but Bacchus is not among those gods for them.
sentences.n: “pars ... pars” is “some ... others”, and both take plural verbs (negant, memorant) although pars is singular — agreement with the sense rather than the form. The sting is the last clause: the sisters will allow the gods everything and still leave this one god out, which is the whole reason for what happens at the end of this part. Magnus prints “et”, “not Bacchus too”, with est understood; some editions print “est”, “Bacchus is not among them”.

sentences.t: Poscitur Alcithoe, postquam siluere sorores.
sentences.l: Alcithoe is called upon, after the sisters fell silent.
sentences.i: Alcithoë is asked for next, now that her sisters have fallen silent.
sentences.n: siluere = siluerunt. The poetic third-person plural perfect in ‑ēre is everywhere in Ovid — the metre likes it — and you will meet it again in this part at enutrivere, genuere, obstrepuere, coepere, habuere, sustinuere. The historic present “poscitur” against that perfect gives the handover its snap.

sentences.t:
Quae radio stantis percurrens stamina telae
“vulgatos taceo” dixit “pastoris amores
Daphnidis Idaei, quem nymphe paelicis ira
contulit in saxum (tantus dolor urit amantes).
sentences.l: And she, running through the threads of the standing loom with her shuttle, said: “I keep silent about the well-known loves of the shepherd Daphnis of Ida, whom a nymph, in anger over a rival-mistress, turned into stone (so great a pain burns lovers).
sentences.i: And she, running her shuttle across the warp of the upright loom, said: “The well-worn loves of Daphnis, the shepherd of Ida, I leave untold — a nymph, in jealousy over a rival, turned him to stone; so fierce is the pain that burns lovers.
sentences.n: “Quae” opening the sentence is a connecting relative: Latin's way of saying “and she”, joining sentences with a pronoun where English starts a new one. It will come again at cuius (290). “paelicis ira”: a paelex is the other woman, a mistress, and the word is a hostile one. The genitive most naturally says what the anger was about — a rival — the nymph being the one supplanted; it can also be read as “a mistress's anger”, and Ovid gives it three words and no more. The parenthesis is Alcithoë's own aside, in the present tense, stepping out of the tale for half a line.

sentences.t:
Nec loquor, ut quondam naturae iure novato
ambiguus fuerit modo vir, modo femina Sithon.
sentences.l: Nor do I tell how once, with the law of nature made new, Sithon was ambiguous — now a man, now a woman.
sentences.i: Nor do I tell how Sithon, once the law of his nature had been made over, was of doubtful sex: now a man, now a woman.
sentences.n: “naturae iure novato” is an ablative absolute — a noun and a participle in the ablative, self-contained, where English wants a clause (“once the law of nature had been remade”). It is one of Ovid's commonest joints and there are six more in this part. “ut ... fuerit” is an indirect question after loquor, hence the subjunctive. Note what she is doing: every tale she says she will skip is a change of sex, and the praeteritio tells them while refusing to.

sentences.t:
Te quoque, nunc adamas, quondam fidissime parvo,
Celmi, Iovi, largoque satos Curetas ab imbri
et Crocon in parvos versum cum Smilace flores
praetereo, dulcique animos novitate tenebo.
sentences.l: You too, Celmis, now adamant, once most faithful to little Jove, and the Curetes sown from a generous rain, and Crocus turned with Smilax into small flowers I pass by, and I shall hold [your] minds with sweet novelty.
sentences.i: You too, Celmis — adamant now, once the most faithful of friends to the infant Jove — and the Curetes sown from a heavy shower, and Crocus, turned with Smilax into little flowers, I pass over: I mean to hold you with a sweet strangeness instead.
sentences.n: “Te ... Celmi” is apostrophe: the speaker turns aside from her audience to address a figure of the tale directly, in the second person, before letting him fall back into the string of accusatives governed by praetereo. The contrast is pointed — “nunc adamas”, the hardest substance there is, against “quondam fidissime”, a boy's loyalty. Here quoque is the plain adverb “too”; elsewhere in the poem the same letters are quō-que, “and with which”, and it is worth checking which one you have.

sentences.t:
Unde sit infamis, quare male fortibus undis
Salmacis enervet tactosque remolliat artus,
discite.
sentences.l: From what source she is ill-famed, why with waters strong to ill effect Salmacis unstrings and re-softens the limbs [she has] touched — learn.
sentences.i: Why Salmacis is ill-famed, why her water, strong to no good end, unstrings a man and leaves the limbs it has touched soft — hear it.
sentences.n: Two indirect questions (unde sit, quare enervet ... remolliat), both subjunctive, hang unresolved across three lines before the single imperative lands on them. “male fortibus” is Latin souring an adjective with an adverb: the water's strength is a strength for harm. “remolliat” keeps its re-: the limbs are made soft again, as though hardness were the thing to be undone — and molli- will run through the whole tale.

sentences.t: Causa latet, vis est notissima fontis.
sentences.l: The cause lies hidden, the power of the spring is most well known.
sentences.i: The cause is hidden; the spring's power everybody knows.
sentences.n: A one-line epigram closing the preamble, two clauses set against each other with no connective at all: the cause hidden, the power best known of anything. It also states the shape of the whole tale — the effect is common knowledge, and the story is the missing explanation. This is an aetiology, and it says so before it starts.

sentences.t:
Mercurio puerum diva Cythereide natum
naides Idaeis enutrivere sub antris;
sentences.l: A boy born to Mercury from the divine Cytherean, the naiads reared beneath Idaean caves;
sentences.i: A boy born to Mercury of the goddess of Cythera was reared by the naiads in the caves of Ida;
sentences.n: natus takes a dative of the father and an ablative of the mother: born to Mercury, of the Cytherean. The mother is not named at all — Venus is called only by her island — and the reticence is deliberate, because the child's name will be built out of his parents' two names. enutrivere = enutriverunt, the ‑ēre perfect again.

sentences.t:
cuius erat facies, in qua materque paterque
cognosci possent; nomen quoque traxit ab illis.
sentences.l: and his was a face in which both mother and father could be recognised; his name too he drew from them.
sentences.i: his face was one in which both mother and father could be made out; his name, too, he took from theirs.
sentences.n: “cuius” is another connecting relative, this time doing genitive duty — “and his”. “possent” is subjunctive in a relative clause of characteristic: not the face in which they were seen but the kind of face in which they could be. Ovid withholds the name for ninety lines and here only points at how it is built, out of Hermes and Aphrodite, legible in the face exactly as in the word.

sentences.t:
Is tria cum primum fecit quinquennia, montes
deseruit patrios, Idaque altrice relicta
ignotis errare locis, ignota videre
flumina gaudebat, studio minuente laborem.
sentences.l: He, as soon as he had made three five-year spans, left his ancestral mountains, and, Ida his nurse having been left behind, rejoiced to wander in unknown places, to see unknown rivers, with eagerness lessening the labour.
sentences.i: As soon as he had made his fifteenth year he left his native mountains, and with Ida his nurse behind him took joy in wandering strange places and seeing strange rivers, his eagerness lessening the effort.
sentences.n: “tria quinquennia” — three five-year spans, Ovid's arithmetical way of saying fifteen, the age at which a Roman boy stood at the edge of manhood. Two ablative absolutes inside four lines: “Ida altrice relicta” with a perfect participle, “studio minuente laborem” with a present one, which is why the second reads as “with his eagerness lessening the toil” rather than “having lessened”. The repeated ignotis ... ignota spreads the unknown across places and rivers alike.

sentences.t:
Ille etiam Lycias urbes Lyciaeque propinquos
Caras adit.
sentences.l: He also approaches the Lycian cities and the Carians neighbouring on Lycia.
sentences.i: He comes, too, to the cities of Lycia and to the Carians who border it.
sentences.n: The unit ends two words into its second line. Ovid's sense-units routinely begin and end in mid-hexameter, and Lectorium follows the punctuation rather than the metre — the verse lines are kept, but the tap-unit is the sentence. “adit” is a historic present dropped among perfects to quicken the travelling.

sentences.t:
Videt hic stagnum lucentis ad imum
usque solum lymphae.
sentences.l: Here he sees a pool of water shining right down to the lowest bottom.
sentences.i: Here he sees a pool whose water is clear all the way down to the floor of it.
sentences.n: “lucentis ... lymphae” is a genitive with stagnum, torn from its noun by the whole prepositional phrase — an order English cannot copy and Latin verse thinks nothing of, and here it stretches the pool's transparency the length of a line and a half. “ad imum usque solum”: all the way to the very floor.

sentences.l: Not there [is] the marsh reed, nor barren sedges, nor rushes with sharp point: the water is see-through;
sentences.i: No marsh reed there, no barren sedge, no rushes with their sharp points: the water is clear through;
sentences.n: Three negatives and no verb at all until “est” arrives with the one positive statement: the absences are catalogued, then the presence named. “acuta cuspide” is an ablative of description, “rushes of sharp point”. The pool is unnaturally clean — nothing grows in it — and that is already a small warning.

sentences.t:
stagni tamen ultima vivo
caespite cinguntur semperque virentibus herbis.
sentences.l: yet the pool's outermost parts are girded with living turf and with grasses always green.
sentences.i: yet the pool's edges are ringed with living turf and grass that is green the year round.
sentences.n: “ultima” is a neuter plural adjective standing on its own as a noun — “the outermost things”, the margins; Latin does this freely where English has to supply a noun. The “tamen” marks the exact contrast: nothing grows in the water, everything grows around it.

sentences.t:
Nympha colit, sed nec venatibus apta, nec arcus
flectere quae soleat nec quae contendere cursu,
solaque naiadum celeri non nota Dianae.
sentences.l: A nymph inhabits [it], but neither fit for hunting, nor one who would be used to bending the bow, nor one who would compete in running, and alone of the naiads not known to swift Diana.
sentences.i: A nymph keeps the place — but no huntress, not the sort to bend a bow or match anyone at running, and the only naiad swift Diana does not know.
sentences.n: “quae soleat ... quae contendere” are relative clauses of characteristic with the subjunctive: not “who does not bend the bow” but “not the kind who would”. The whole introduction is by negation, and every negative says the same thing — she is not Diana's sort. For a nymph in this poem, refusing the hunt is refusing chastity, and Ovid lets the reader do the arithmetic.

sentences.t:
Saepe suas illi fama est dixisse sorores:
“Salmaci, vel iaculum vel pictas sume pharetras,
et tua cum duris venatibus otia misce.”
sentences.l: Often, the report is, her own sisters said to her: “Salmacis, take up either the javelin or the painted quivers, and mix your leisure with hard hunting.”
sentences.i: Often, the story goes, her sisters told her: “Salmacis, take up a javelin, take up the painted quiver — mix a little hard hunting into your idleness.”
sentences.n: “fama est” with an accusative and infinitive (sorores dixisse) is Ovid sourcing a report he does not vouch for: the story goes. “Salmaci” is the vocative of a Greek name in ‑is. The jab is in “otia”: otium is leisure with a faint reproach already in it, set against the hunt's duris.

sentences.t:
Nec iaculum sumit nec pictas illa pharetras,
nec sua cum duris venatibus otia miscet,
sentences.l: She takes up neither the javelin nor the painted quivers, nor does she mix her leisure with hard hunting,
sentences.i: She takes up no javelin and no painted quiver, and mixes no hard hunting into her idleness,
sentences.n: The refusal is made by repeating the sisters' own words back in the indicative — sume becomes sumit, misce becomes miscet — with no word for “no” anywhere but the nec. The unit is left deliberately open: the “sed” that answers it is in the next.

sentences.l: but now she washes her beautiful limbs in her own spring, often draws down her hair with a Cytorian comb, and — what may suit her — consults the waters she has gazed into;
sentences.i: but now bathes her lovely limbs in her own pool, often draws a Cytorian comb through her hair, and asks the water she has been staring into what suits her;
sentences.n: “quid se deceat” is an indirect question tucked inside the sentence, subjunctive, and the water is what she puts it to. Cytorus in Paphlagonia was famous for its boxwood, so the comb is named by the mountain its material came from — a small learned flourish of the kind Ovid cannot resist. “spectatas ... undas” matters: the water has already been gazed at before it is consulted. The mirror is a habit.

sentences.l: now, wrapped as to her body in a see-through robe, she lies on soft leaves or on soft grasses; often she gathers flowers.
sentences.i: now, her body wrapped in a translucent robe, she lies down on soft leaves or soft grass; often she gathers flowers.
sentences.n: “circumdata corpus” is the Greek accusative of respect: the participle is passive and the accusative says in what respect — wrapped round as to her body. English can only manage “her body wrapped”; the construction is a Grecism Ovid is fond of and it will recur in the poem. “mollibus ... mollibus” plants the word this tale ends on. And the catalogue of her idleness closes on flower-gathering, which is never idle in this poem — it is what a girl is doing in the moment before she is seized, as Europa was gathering flowers at the end of Book II. Here the gatherer is the one who will take.

sentences.t:
Et tunc quoque forte legebat,
cum puerum vidit visumque optavit habere.
sentences.l: And then too she happened to be gathering, when she saw the boy and, [him] seen, wished to have [him].
sentences.i: And she happened to be gathering then too, when she saw the boy — and, having seen him, wanted him.
sentences.n: The inverted cum: the imperfect legebat lays out the scene and the perfect in the cum-clause breaks in on it, so the emphasis falls on the interruption rather than on the setting. “visumque optavit habere” folds two stages into a participle — the seeing and the wanting are one motion — and habere, “to have”, is blunt about what the wanting is for.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen ante adiit, etsi properabat adire,
quam se conposuit, quam circumspexit amictus,
et finxit vultum et meruit formosa videri.
sentences.l: Nor yet did she approach before — though she was hurrying to approach — she had composed herself, had looked over her robes, and shaped her face, and deserved to be seen as beautiful.
sentences.i: She did not go to him, though she was in haste to go, until she had set herself in order, looked her dress over, arranged her face, and earned the right to be seen as beautiful.
sentences.n: “ante ... quam” is split across two lines, with “etsi properabat adire” wedged into the gap: the delay is enacted by the word order before it is described. Magnus prints “conposuit”, and the edition's unassimilated spellings (conp-, adp-, inm-, adl-) are kept as printed throughout. The sting is “meruit formosa videri” — she does not simply look beautiful, she works at it until she has earned the look.

sentences.t:
Tum sic orsa loqui: “Puer o dignissime credi
esse deus, seu tu deus es, potes esse Cupido,
sentences.l: Then she began thus to speak: “O boy most worthy to be believed to be a god, if you are a god, you may be Cupid;
sentences.i: Then she began: “Boy — you deserve to be taken for a god; if you are a god, you may well be Cupid;
sentences.n: “orsa [est] loqui”: ordior is deponent, so its perfect participle is active in sense — “having begun”, i.e. she began. The vocative “Puer o dignissime” with the o postponed is high style, and every word of the compliment is calculated: she has already decided what answer she wants.

sentences.t:
sive es mortalis, qui te genuere, beati,
et frater felix, et fortunata profecto,
siqua tibi soror est, et quae dedit ubera nutrix:
sentences.l: but if you are mortal, blessed [are] they who begot you, and happy [your] brother, and fortunate indeed, if you have any sister, and the nurse who gave [you] her breasts:
sentences.i: but if you are mortal, then blessed are those who begot you, and happy your brother, and fortunate indeed your sister, if you have one, and the nurse who gave you her breast —
sentences.n: genuere = genuerunt. Four blessings and hardly a verb among them — beati, felix, fortunata all stand without an “est”, which Latin drops freely, and the omissions give the flattery its rush. The list has a shape — it climbs through the family so that the one place left unfilled, the wife's, is the place she means to take.

sentences.t:
sed longe cunctis longeque beatior illa,
siqua tibi sponsa est, siquam dignabere taeda.
sentences.l: but far, far more blessed than all of them [is] she, if there is any betrothed of yours, if you shall deem any woman worthy of the marriage-torch.
sentences.i: but far, far happier than any of them is she — if you are promised to anyone, or will think anyone worth the wedding torch.
sentences.n: “dignabere” is the future of the deponent dignor, with the alternative second-person ending ‑bere for ‑beris that verse prefers. “taeda” is the pine torch carried in the wedding procession and stands for the marriage itself — plain metonymy, and it lets her name what she wants without naming it.

sentences.t:
Haec tibi sive aliqua est, mea sit furtiva voluptas,
seu nulla est, ego sim, thalamumque ineamus eundem.”
sentences.l: If there is some such woman for you, let my pleasure be a stolen one; or if there is none, let me be [her], and let us enter the same bedchamber.”
sentences.i: If there is such a woman, let what I take be stolen; if there is none, let it be me — and let us go to the same bed.”
sentences.n: Three jussive subjunctives (sit, sim, ineamus) turn flattery into a proposition in a line and a half. “furtiva voluptas” is “thieving pleasure”, the standard elegiac phrase for an affair conducted behind someone's back: she offers adultery first and marriage as the fallback. There is no question anywhere in it — she tells him what will happen.

sentences.t: Nais ab his tacuit.
sentences.l: The naiad fell silent after these things.
sentences.i: With that the naiad stopped.
sentences.n: “ab his” is “from these [words]”, the preposition doing what English does with “after” or “with that”. Four words between two long sentences: Ovid lets the silence land before the boy's face answers for him.

sentences.t:
Pueri rubor ora notavit
(nescit enim, quid amor), sed et erubuisse decebat.
sentences.l: A blush marked the boy's face (for he does not know what love [is]), but even to have blushed became him.
sentences.i: A blush marked the boy's face — he does not know what love is — but even blushing became him.
sentences.n: “nescit ... quid amor [sit]” is an indirect question with the verb simply left out, and it is in the present: the narrator steps out of the past to say what is true of him. That parenthesis is the whole case for everything that follows — he is not refusing coyly, he does not understand what is being asked. “erubuisse decebat” makes a perfect infinitive the subject of decebat: not the blushing but the having-blushed suited him.

sentences.t:
Hic color aprica pendentibus arbore pomis
aut ebori tincto est, aut sub candore rubenti,
cum frustra resonant aera auxiliaria, lunae.
sentences.l: This colour belongs to apples hanging on a sunny tree, or to stained ivory, or to the moon reddening beneath her whiteness, when the helping bronzes ring out in vain.
sentences.i: It is the colour of apples on a sunlit bough, or of ivory stained, or of the moon reddening under her own brightness while the bronzes clash to help her and cannot.
sentences.n: “lunae” is held to the last word of the third line, far from the datives it belongs with — the sentence is a small suspense with the answer at the end. Romans beat bronze during an eclipse to help the labouring moon; “frustra” is the narrator's verdict on the practice, and it quietly makes the third comparison the colour of something being lost. “sub candore rubenti”: the red is under the white and shows through it.

sentences.t:
Poscenti nymphae sine fine sororia saltem
oscula iamque manus ad eburnea colla ferenti
“desinis? aut fugio, tecumque” ait “ista relinquo.”
sentences.l: To the nymph demanding without end at least sisterly kisses and already bringing her hands to his ivory neck: “Will you stop? Or I flee, and with you” he says “I leave these things of yours.”
sentences.i: To the nymph who kept demanding, endlessly, at least a sister's kisses, and was already bringing her hands to his ivory neck, he says: “Will you stop? Or I go — and leave this place of yours, and you with it.”
sentences.n: Two long present participles in the dative (poscenti, ferenti) carry two whole lines of her behaviour before the boy is given a word, and the datives hang unattached until “ait” finally arrives. “sororia oscula” is her own euphemism and “saltem” gives it away: a sister's kisses are what she will settle for. “ista” is the demonstrative of the second person, “those things of yours” — he hands her back her own place. Magnus prints “aut fugio”, a threat, “or I flee”; some editions print “an fugio”, which makes it a second question, “or am I to go?” — the difference between a boy who threatens and a boy who pleads.

sentences.t:
Salmacis extimuit “loca” que “haec tibi libera trado,
hospes” ait, simulatque gradu discedere verso,
tunc quoque respiciens, fruticumque recondita silva
delituit, flexuque genu submisit.
sentences.l: Salmacis took fright: “These places I hand over to you free, stranger,” she says, and pretends to depart with her step turned, then too looking back, and hidden in a thicket of bushes she lay concealed, and sank her knee in a bend.
sentences.i: Salmacis took fright. “The place is yours, stranger, and freely,” she says — and pretends to go, turning on her heel, still looking back even then; and hidden away in a thicket she crouched, one knee bent under her.
sentences.n: The enclitic ‑que has to attach to a word, so Magnus prints it fastened to the quoted “loca” — “loca” que — and the quotation is broken open around it. “gradu verso” is another ablative absolute, “with her step turned”. Everything after “extimuit” is a lie: “libera trado” is the formal language of handing over property, a host's courtesy, and she means none of it — the very next word is that she was still looking back.

sentences.t:
At ille,
scilicet ut vacuis et inobservatus in herbis,
huc it et hinc illuc, et in adludentibus undis
summa pedum taloque tenus vestigia tingit;
sentences.l: But he, unobserved of course and in empty grass, goes this way and from here to there, and in the waters playing about [him] dips the topmost soles of his feet — and that as far as the ankle;
sentences.i: But he — unwatched, of course, and alone in the empty grass — goes this way and that, and dips no more than the soles of his feet in the water that laps about him, and then goes in ankle-deep;
sentences.n: “scilicet” is the narrator's irony: he supposes himself unobserved, and we have just watched her hide. “summa ... vestigia” is one phrase, “the topmost soles”, with “pedum” and the whole “talo tenus” wedged inside it, so the depth of the wading is spoken twice in one line and deepens between the two: first only the undersides of the feet, then the ankle. “tenus” is a postposition, following the ablative it governs. “adludentibus undis” gives the water a verb of play: it is a participant before Salmacis is.

sentences.t:
nec mora, temperie blandarum captus aquarum
mollia de tenero velamina corpore ponit.
sentences.l: and no delay — caught by the mildness of the coaxing waters, he lays soft coverings from his tender body.
sentences.i: and with no delay, caught by the mildness of the coaxing water, he takes the soft coverings from his young body.
sentences.n: “nec mora” is a stock narrative accelerator with no verb at all, dropped in like a stage direction. “blandarum” is the adjective for a flatterer, so the water coaxes exactly as Salmacis coaxed; and “captus”, “caught”, is a hunting word, used of him at the moment he thinks himself safe. mollia arrives for the third time.

sentences.t:
Tum vero placuit, nudaeque cupidine formae
Salmacis exarsit: flagrant quoque lumina nymphae,
non aliter quam cum puro nitidissimus orbe
opposita speculi referitur imagine Phoebus.
sentences.l: Then indeed he pleased, and with desire of the naked form Salmacis blazed up: the nymph's eyes flame too, not otherwise than when Phoebus, most brilliant in a clear disc, is struck back by the answering image of a mirror.
sentences.i: Then indeed he pleased her, and Salmacis caught fire with desire for the naked body: the nymph's eyes flame too, no otherwise than when Phoebus, at his brightest in a clear disc, is flung back by a mirror held up against him.
sentences.n: “cupidine formae” is an objective genitive — desire directed at the form, not the form's own desire. “exarsit” and “flagrant” put the fire in her before anything has been done, and then the simile makes her eyes not the source of the light but the reflector: what comes off her is his own brightness doubled. “referitur” is the passive of referio, “is struck back” — the physics of reflection taken literally.

sentences.t:
Vixque moram patitur, vix iam sua gaudia differt,
iam cupit amplecti, iam se male continet amens.
sentences.l: And scarcely does she endure delay, scarcely now does she put off her joys, now she desires to embrace, now, out of her mind, she holds herself in badly.
sentences.i: She can hardly bear the wait, hardly put her pleasure off any longer; now she wants to take hold of him, now, out of her senses, she barely keeps herself back.
sentences.n: Two “vix” and three “iam” inside two lines, each one starting a fresh clause — the metre is losing patience along with her. “se male continet” uses male as line 285 used it (“male fortibus”): the adverb sours whatever it touches, so this is holding-in done badly. “amens”, out of one's mind, is this poem's standard word for desire that has stopped calculating.

sentences.t:
Ille cavis velox adplauso corpore palmis
desilit in latices, alternaque bracchia ducens
in liquidis translucet aquis, ut eburnea siquis
signa tegat claro vel candida lilia vitro.
sentences.l: He, swift, with his body clapped by hollowed palms, leaps down into the water, and drawing his arms alternately shines through in the clear waters, as if someone should cover ivory figures, or white lilies, with transparent glass.
sentences.i: He claps his hollowed palms against his body, leaps swiftly into the water, and, drawing arm after arm, shows through the clear water as ivory figures do, or white lilies, when someone has covered them with clear glass.
sentences.n: “adplauso corpore palmis” is an ablative absolute recording the exact gesture — the swimmer's slap of cupped hands on the body before the dive. “translucet” is the point of the whole description: the pool that hid nothing at 298 now displays him. Both halves of the simile are white things a person owns and looks at, and “eburnea” has already been used of his neck at 335.

sentences.t:
“Vicimus et meus est!” exclamat nais et omni
veste procul iacta mediis inmittitur undis,
sentences.l: “We have won and he is mine!” cries the naiad, and, all her clothing flung far off, she is launched into the middle of the waters,
sentences.i: “We have won! He is mine!” cries the naiad, and, every garment flung away, throws herself into the middle of the water,
sentences.n: “vicimus” is a plural for a single speaker, the tone of a general's dispatch: she announces her own victory before it has happened. “omni veste procul iacta” is one more ablative absolute, and it mirrors his own undressing ten lines earlier, which was what undid him. “inmittitur” is passive in form and reflexive in force — she launches herself.

sentences.l: and holds him fighting and plucks struggling kisses, and thrusts her hands beneath and touches his unwilling breast, and now on this side, now on that, she pours herself round the youth;
sentences.i: and holds him as he fights, and snatches kisses he struggles against, and forces her hands under him and touches his unwilling chest, and pours herself round the young man, now on this side of him, now on that;
sentences.n: The adjectives do the refusing: pugnantem, luctantia, invita — the kisses themselves struggle and the chest itself is unwilling, a transferred epithet that puts his resistance into every separate part of him. “carpit” is the verb for picking flowers, and picking flowers is what she was doing when she saw him. “circumfunditur” is again passive in form and active in sense: she pours herself around him, which is what water does.

sentences.t:
denique nitentem contra elabique volentem
inplicat, ut serpens, quam regia sustinet ales
sublimemque rapit: pendens caput illa pedesque
adligat et cauda spatiantes inplicat alas:
sentences.l: at last she entwines him as he strains against her and wishes to slip away, like a serpent which the royal bird holds up and snatches aloft: hanging, she [the snake] binds head and feet and with her tail entwines the outspread wings:
sentences.i: at last she winds herself round him as he strains against her and wants to slip free — as a snake does, held up by the royal bird and snatched aloft: hanging there, it binds head and feet and winds its tail round the spread wings:
sentences.n: “regia ales” is the eagle, named by its rank rather than its name, as Ovid names most things. Notice who is who in the simile: the snake is the one being carried off, and yet it is the snake that binds and entwines — so the eagle's victim is the image for the attacker here, and the boy is left standing for the bird. “inplicat” is used of Salmacis and then of the snake, sealing the comparison with the repeated verb.

sentences.t:
utve solent hederae longos intexere truncos,
utque sub aequoribus deprensum polypus hostem
continet, ex omni dimissis parte flagellis.
sentences.l: or as ivies are accustomed to weave through long trunks, and as beneath the waters the octopus holds an enemy it has caught, with its tendrils let down from every side.
sentences.i: or as ivy weaves its way up long trunks, or as the octopus beneath the sea holds the prey it has caught, its arms let down on every side.
sentences.n: Three similes in a row, and each is tighter than the last: bird and snake, ivy and tree, octopus and prey — sky, then tree, then sea floor, ending on the one image with no escape in it. “deprensum ... hostem” catches the object with a participle before the sentence names it. “dimissis flagellis” is the last ablative absolute of the series; flagellum is a whip or a plant's runner, and Ovid puts it to the arms.

sentences.t:
Perstat Atlantiades, sperataque gaudia nymphae
denegat.
sentences.l: The descendant of Atlas holds out, and denies the nymph the joys she hoped for.
sentences.i: Atlas's descendant holds out, and refuses the nymph the pleasure she had hoped for.
sentences.n: “Atlantiades” reaches back two generations through his father: Mercury was the son of Maia, daughter of Atlas. The divine line is invoked at the moment the boy is least able to use it. “Perstat” placed first is the whole of his resistance, one verb, against four lines of hers; and “sperata gaudia” answers the “sua gaudia” she could hardly defer at 350.

sentences.t:
Illa premit, commissaque corpore toto
sicut inhaerebat, “pugnes licet, inprobe” dixit,
“non tamen effugies.
sentences.l: She presses on, and, joined to him with her whole body and clinging as she was, “Fight though you may, shameless one,” she said, “you will not escape all the same.
sentences.i: She presses on, fastened to him with her whole body, clinging as she was. “Fight if you like, you shameless thing,” she said, “you will not get away.
sentences.n: “pugnes licet” is licet with the subjunctive — a concessive, “granted that you fight”, “fight as you may”. “inprobe” is worth stopping on: it is what a Roman said to someone shameless, greedy, past all restraint, and it is her word for the boy who will not give in while she holds him down. The word belongs to her, and it is doing her work, not the narrator's.

sentences.t:
Ita di iubeatis! et istum
nulla dies a me nec me diducat ab isto.”
sentences.l: So may you order it, gods! and let no day part him from me nor me from him.”
sentences.i: Gods, so order it! And let no day part him from me, or me from him.”
sentences.n: A prayer in two jussive subjunctives (iubeatis, diducat), and the poem's usual cruelty is to grant the words rather than the wish. “istum ... isto” is the demonstrative of the second person, “that one of yours, there”: even inside her prayer she points at him instead of naming him. And the chiasmus — him from me, me from him — is already the shape the two bodies are about to take.

sentences.t:
Vota suos habuere deos: nam mixta duorum
corpora iunguntur, faciesque inducitur illis
una, velut, siquis conducat cortice ramos,
crescendo iungi pariterque adolescere cernit.
sentences.l: The prayers had gods of their own: for the mingled bodies of the two are joined, and one face is drawn over them, just as, if someone should bring branches together under bark, he sees them joined in the growing and ripening alike.
sentences.i: The prayer found gods of its own: for the two bodies are mingled and joined, and one face is drawn over them both — as when a man binds branches under a single bark and sees them grow together and come on as one.
sentences.n: habuere = habuerunt. “Vota suos habuere deos” is five words and bitter: the prayer got the gods it deserved, not the gods that would have been just. The simile is grafting — a gardener's operation — so what is done to the boy is described as horticulture, done to a plant, by someone, on purpose. “siquis conducat ... cernit” is a general condition with subjunctive in the if-clause and indicative in the main.

sentences.t:
Sic ubi conplexu coierunt membra tenaci,
nec duo sunt et forma duplex, nec femina dici
nec puer ut possit: neutrumque et utrumque videntur.
sentences.l: So when the limbs had come together in a clinging embrace, they are not two, and the form is double, so that it can be called neither woman nor boy: they seem neither and both.
sentences.i: So, once the limbs had come together in that clinging hold, they are not two, and the shape is double — it can be called neither woman nor boy: it seems neither and it seems both.
sentences.n: coierunt is the full form of the perfect Ovid has been printing as ‑ēre all through this part. The Latin is built to refuse a category: “nec duo sunt et forma duplex” says not-two and double in one breath, and “neutrumque et utrumque” sets neither beside both with ‑que ... et, which is the ordinary way of saying “both A and B”. “videntur” stays plural although what it describes is now one body: the literal keeps that plural (“they seem”), the idiomatic resolves it to “it”, and the gap between the two lines is exactly the difficulty the Latin is refusing to settle.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi se liquidas, quo vir descenderat, undas
semimarem fecisse videt, mollitaque in illis
membra, manus tendens, sed non iam voce virili,
Hermaphroditus ait:
sentences.l: So when he sees that the clear waters, into which he had gone down a man, have made him half-male, and his limbs softened in them, stretching out his hands, but no longer with a man's voice, Hermaphroditus says:
sentences.i: So when he sees that the clear water, into which he had gone down a man, has made him half male, and his limbs softened in it, he stretches out his hands — but no longer in a man's voice — and Hermaphroditus says:
sentences.n: The name is held to the head of the fourth line, the last thing before he speaks: the boy is not called Hermaphroditus until he is one. “se ... fecisse” is an accusative and infinitive after videt, with the subject-accusative torn from its infinitive by the whole relative clause “quo vir descenderat”, which is where the sentence keeps the word “man”. “semimarem”, half-male, is the word the poem chooses; “mollita” brings back the softness that has been in this water since 314.

sentences.t:
“Nato date munera vestro,
et pater et genetrix, amborum nomen habenti:
quisquis in hos fontes vir venerit, exeat inde
semivir et tactis subito mollescat in undis.”
sentences.l: “Give gifts to your son, both father and mother, to him who has the name of you both: whatever man shall have come into these springs, let him go out from there half a man and let him suddenly soften in the waters he has touched.”
sentences.i: “Give your son a gift, father and mother both, since he carries the name of you both: let any man who comes into this water go out of it half a man, and go soft the moment the water touches him.”
sentences.n: The prayer is framed as an exchange — he names himself by the gift his parents already made him, the name, and asks another in the same breath. “quisquis ... venerit” is a future perfect in the relative clause with jussive subjunctives in the main: whoever will have come, let him go out. Note what he does not ask: not to be restored, but that it happen to everyone — and that is the aetiology promised at 285–287. “semivir” answers “semimarem” of four lines before and is the harder word: a Roman insult.

sentences.t:
Motus uterque parens nati rata verba biformis
fecit et incesto fontem medicamine tinxit.”
sentences.l: Moved, each parent made the words of their two-formed son ratified, and stained the spring with an unclean drug.”
sentences.i: Both parents were moved, and made their two-formed son's words good, and steeped the spring with a foul infusion.”
sentences.n: “rata ... fecit”: ratus is the word for a thing formally confirmed, as a treaty is ratified. The gods do not grant the prayer, they validate it. “incesto ... medicamine” is the narrator's judgment and not the parents' — incestus is impure, unholy, and medicamen is a drug or a dye, so the spring is doctored rather than blessed. The closing quotation mark ends Alcithoë's tale, which opened at 276.

sentences.t: Finis erat dictis.
sentences.l: There was an end to the words.
sentences.i: The telling was over.
sentences.n: Three words, closing the tale as briefly as “Nais ab his tacuit” closed the speech inside it at 329. The imperfect “erat” leaves the scene running instead of shutting it: the tale ends, the sisters do not.

sentences.t:
Sed adhuc Minyeia proles
urget opus spernitque deum festumque profanat,
tympana cum subito non adparentia raucis
obstrepuere sonis, et adunco tibia cornu
tinnulaque aera sonant;
sentences.l: But still the offspring of Minyas presses the work and scorns the god and profanes the festival, when suddenly drums not appearing thundered against [them] with hoarse sounds, and the pipe with its curved horn and the jangling bronzes sound;
sentences.i: But the daughters of Minyas keep pressing the work, and scorn the god, and profane his festival — when suddenly drums that no one can see thundered out with hoarse noise, and the pipe with its curving horn and the clashing bronzes sound;
sentences.n: Another inverted cum: three present-tense verbs of defiance run on until the cum-clause breaks in with a perfect, obstrepuere (= obstrepuerunt), so the interruption is grammatical before it is narrative. “non adparentia” — not appearing: there are no drums there, and the god arrives as sound without a source. The instruments are Bacchus's own, tympanum, curved pipe, cymbals — the rites the sisters would not attend, now inside the house with them.

sentences.t:
redolent murraeque crocique,
resque fide maior, coepere virescere telae
inque hederae faciem pendens frondescere vestis.
sentences.l: myrrh and saffron give off scent, and — a thing greater than belief — the webs began to grow green, and the hanging cloth to put out leaves into the likeness of ivy.
sentences.i: myrrh and saffron give off their scent, and — past believing — the webs began to turn green, and the hanging cloth to leaf out into the likeness of ivy.
sentences.n: “res fide maior” is a parenthetical nominative with no verb, the narrator's own aside: a thing greater than trust. coepere = coeperunt. The change begins in the weaving — the work they preferred to the god turns into the god's own plant, and the loom that has framed all the sisters' tales is the first thing to go.

sentences.l: Part goes off into vines, and what were lately threads are changed into vine-shoot; from the warp a tendril comes out; the purple fits its brightness to the painted grapes.
sentences.i: Part of it goes off into vines; what were threads a moment ago are turned to vine-shoots; a tendril comes out of the warp; the purple lends its brightness to the painted grapes.
sentences.n: “quae modo fila fuerunt” — the relative is neuter plural, taking its number and gender from the noun it is being equated to rather than from anything before it. The dye is the wittiest touch: the cloth's purple is exactly the colour grapes need, so the weaving is not destroyed but repurposed, and even the sisters' craft is conscripted for Bacchus.

sentences.t:
Iamque dies exactus erat, tempusque subibat,
quod tu nec tenebras nec possis dicere lucem,
sed cum luce tamen dubiae confinia noctis:
sentences.l: And now the day had been driven through, and there was coming on the time which you could call neither darkness nor light, but the borders of doubtful night together with light:
sentences.i: And now the day was spent, and there was coming on the hour you could call neither dark nor light, but the border of an uncertain night that still holds light:
sentences.n: “tu ... possis” is the generalising second person with a potential subjunctive — “you” meaning anyone, a way of drawing the reader in without turning aside to address them. “dies exactus erat”: exigo is used of driving a thing right through to its end, so the day is not merely over but finished off. All three lines are one periphrasis for dusk, and the refusal to give it a name prepares a creature that is not one thing or the other either.

sentences.t:
tecta repente quati pinguesque ardere videntur
lampades et rutilis conlucere ignibus aedes
falsaque saevarum simulacra ululare ferarum.
sentences.l: the roofs seem suddenly to be shaken and the fat torches to burn and the house to blaze all through with red fires and false likenesses of savage beasts to howl.
sentences.i: suddenly the roof seems to shake, the oiled torches to catch, the house to blaze red through and through, and false shapes of wild beasts to howl.
sentences.n: One “videntur” governs four infinitives (quati, ardere, conlucere, ululare) and holds the whole apparition at arm's length: everything here is what seems to happen. “falsa simulacra” says outright that the beasts are not there — in this poem Bacchus works by illusion before he works on bodies. “pingues lampades” are torches fat with pitch.

sentences.t:
Fumida iamdudum latitant per tecta sorores,
diversaeque locis ignes ac lumina vitant;
sentences.l: For a long while now the sisters keep hiding through the smoky house, and, apart in [different] places, avoid the fires and the lights;
sentences.i: For some time now the sisters have been hiding about the smoke-filled house, and, scattered to separate corners, avoid the flames and the lights;
sentences.n: “iamdudum” with a present tense is an idiom English has to turn into a perfect: they have been hiding for a while and still are. “latitant” is the frequentative of lateo — not “hide” but “keep hiding”, scurrying from one place to another. Avoiding the light is the first bat-behaviour, and it arrives before any change of body.

sentences.t:
dumque petunt tenebras, parvos membrana per artus
porrigitur tenuique includit bracchia pinna.
sentences.l: and while they seek the shadows, a membrane is stretched across their small limbs and shuts their arms in with a thin wing.
sentences.i: and as they make for the dark, a membrane spreads over their shrunken limbs and closes their arms inside a thin wing.
sentences.n: “dum” takes the present indicative even inside past narrative — Latin keeps dum-clauses in the present and the surrounding tense does not touch them. The limbs are “parvos” before anything has been said about shrinking: the smallness is reported as already accomplished, which is how Ovid does most of his transformations — by noticing rather than by describing.

sentences.t:
Nec qua perdiderint veterem ratione figuram
scire sinunt tenebrae.
sentences.l: Nor does the darkness allow [them] to know by what means they lost their old shape.
sentences.i: Nor does the dark let them know by what means they lost the shape they had.
sentences.n: An indirect question (qua ratione perdiderint) with the subjunctive, and “ratione” is torn three words away from its “qua” — the phrase is broken apart exactly as the shape is. The darkness they went looking for is the reason they cannot see what is being done to them, which is worse than being watched.

sentences.t:
Non illas pluma levavit,
sustinuere tamen se perlucentibus alis;
sentences.l: No feather lifted them, yet they held themselves up on translucent wings;
sentences.n: sustinuere = sustinuerunt, the ‑ēre perfect one last time. The line insists on what they are not: this is a bat, defined against a bird, and Ovid never names the animal — he describes until the reader supplies the word. “perlucentibus” is the adjective used of Salmacis's robe at 313, so the last transformation of the day borrows the vocabulary of the tale just told.

sentences.t:
conataeque loqui minimam et pro corpore vocem
emittunt, peraguntque leves stridore querellas.
sentences.l: and having tried to speak they send out a voice smallest and in keeping with their body, and carry through their light complaints in a squeak.
sentences.i: and, trying to speak, they let out the tiniest voice, one to match their body, and carry their small complaints through in a squeak.
sentences.n: “conatae” is the perfect participle of a deponent, so it is active in sense — “having tried”, not “having been tried”; perosae in the next unit is the same. “pro corpore” is “in proportion to the body”, the voice scaled down with the frame. Magnus prints “leves ... querellas”, making the complaints light; some editions print “levi stridore”, making the squeak light instead — the same two words, hooked up the other way round.

sentences.t:
Tectaque, non silvas celebrant lucemque perosae
nocte volant, seroque tenent a vespere nomen.
sentences.l: And they haunt houses, not woods, and, having thoroughly hated the light, they fly by night, and take their name from the late evening.
sentences.i: And it is houses they throng, not woods; hating the light, they fly by night, and take their name from the lateness of evening.
sentences.n: “perosae” is another deponent participle with active force, and the per- makes the hatred total. The last line explains the Latin name without ever printing it — vespertilio, the bat, from vesper, evening — so the tale of women who would not keep a festival ends, exactly as the tale inside it ended, in a word.

questions: House rendering proposed, IV.378–379 (nec duo sunt et forma duplex, nec femina dici / nec puer ut possit: neutrumque et utrumque videntur) — the most quoted lines in the part. Shipped l: “they are not two, and the form is double, so that it can be called neither woman nor boy: they seem neither and both.” Shipped i: “they are not two, and the shape is double — it can be called neither woman nor boy: it seems neither and it seems both.” Please ratify or replace. The open point inside it: videntur is plural though the subject is now one body, and I kept the plural in l and resolved it to a singular “it” in i.

House rendering proposed, IV.373a (Vota suos habuere deos) — quoted on its own as a sententia. Shipped l: “The prayers had gods of their own”; shipped i: “The prayer found gods of its own.” I deliberately avoided the smoother “her prayers found their gods” because it arrived already finished; please ratify or replace.

House rendering proposed, IV.287b (Causa latet, vis est notissima fontis) — quoted as the epigram of the episode. Shipped l: “The cause lies hidden, the power of the spring is most well known”; shipped i: “The cause is hidden; the spring's power everybody knows.” (Review changed the shipped i from “is notorious”, which imported an ill-fame that notissima does not carry and read as a ready-made anthology phrase.)

Advisory call I am not fully sure of: trigger 1 (sexual violence) plainly fires and is the lede's first clause. I also folded in a second clause for trigger 2 — the part is an aetiology of a body that is neither male nor female, and the boy's name is the source of a word still applied to intersex people — rather than opening a separate advisory, since the contract allows one lede to name both. If the ruling is that trigger 2 covers only aetiologies of a named people's character, the second clause should be cut and the point left to `more`.

Variant judged sense-changing, IV.336: Magnus “aut fugio” (or I flee — a threat) against The Latin Library's “an fugio” (or am I to flee? — a second question). Noted in n; it changes the boy's tone at the one moment he speaks for himself.
Variant judged sense-changing, IV.413: Magnus “leves ... querellas” (the complaints are light) against “levi stridore” (the squeak is light). Noted in n.

Variant noted as marginal, IV.273: Magnus “et” (sed non et Bacchus in illis, with est understood) against “est”. The sense barely moves, but the line is the hinge of the frame, so I gave it one clause. Say if that is over-noting.

The other fifteen flagged variants (auris/aures, tunc/tum ×3, Tum/tunc, si qua / siqua ×3, tingit/tinguit, si quis / siquis ×2, diducat/deducat, the position of iam at 382, Sed/et at 389, urget/urguet) I treated as orthography, morphology or word order and passed over in silence.

Homograph, aera (IV.333, IV.393): here the neuter plural of aes, bronze — the eclipse-gongs and then Bacchus's cymbals — not the accusative singular of aer, air, which is what the same letters give elsewhere in the poem. Worth a distinct glossary sense.
Homograph, ora (IV.329): neuter plural of os, the face, not the plural of ora, shore. The poem uses both.
Homograph, telae / telas (IV.275, IV.394): the loom and the web it holds, from tela — not the plural of telum, weapon, which stands very close to it in the glossary.
Homograph, signa (IV.355): carved figures, statues — not signs or military standards.

No damaged digitization found in these 145 lines. Every unusual form parses as an edition spelling rather than OCR damage: conposuit, adplauso, adludentibus, adcommodat, adligat, adparentia, conlucere, conplexu, inmittitur, inplicat, inprobe, querellas, murrae. All kept as printed.

Ambiguity a human should rule on, IV.277 (nymphe paelicis ira): the genitive can be objective (anger over a rival — the nymph is the supplanted lover) or subjective (the anger of a mistress). Review shipped the objective reading in l and i and flagged both in n. Ovid gives no context here, and the sense turns on which woman is the paelex.

Review edit to the advisory lede: the second trigger is now named plainly — the word hermaphrodite and intersex people — where the draft said only “the word taken from the boy's name”. If the ruling is that trigger 2 does not fire on this part, cut that clause rather than re-soften it.

Number check: this part never says how many daughters of Minyas there are. It has only Alcithoe, sorores and Minyeia proles. Review removed “three” from about and from the advisory. If the library wants the number, it has to come from the earlier part of Book IV, not from here.

Convention question: discite at IV.287 is an imperative to learn, and “learn” is a word the app's own voice avoids. I kept “learn” in l, where transparency governs, and used “hear it” in i. Confirm that the ban is on Lectorium's language and never on Ovid's.
